newsitem.title: LEBANON: Solidere seeks non-Arab finance for Beirut.
newsitem.headline: Solidere seeks non-Arab finance for Beirut.

text.p: Solidere, the $2 billion real estate company that is rebuilding Beirut, Tuesday offered non-Arabs their first chance to invest in the reconstruction of Lebanon's capital city.
Market sources in Beirut said Solidere began marketing Global Depository Receipts worth $115 million to $125 million, giving non-Arabs the right to invest in Lebanon's biggest company.
"They are making an international offering of 10 million GDRs for an issue size of $125 million," a source told Reuters. The planned issue date was Nov. 26, he said.
A Solidere executive declined to comment about the issue.
The Solidere project is the flagship of billionaire Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri's multi-billion-dollar drive to rebuild Lebanon from the ruins of the 1975-1990 civil war.

The company began work on rebuilding Beirut's war-shattered city centre, an area covering 400 acres (1.6 million square meters), in late 1994. It plans to develop 5.28 million square yards (4.4 million square meters) of floor space.
Huge swathes of war-damaged buildings have already been demolished and much of the infrastructure work has been done. Several buildings of architectural value have also been restored.
The company calls the project, which is expected to be completed in 25 years, the world's biggest urban redevelopment project.

But non-Arab investors have until now been unable to participate, since Lebanese law bars them from buying real estate in the country. Solidere's oversubscribed $650 million share flotation in January 1994 was restricted to Lebanese and Arab investors.

GDRs are receipts that can be readily traded abroad, avoiding the registration complications of trading the underlying shares they represent. However, because of ownership restrictions, the Solidere GDRs would represent an economic interest in the underlying shares, rather than the shares themselves, the sources said.
Each GDR would be worth one-tenth of one of Solidere's shares. The company's A and B shares traded on the Beirut Stock Exchange Tuesday at $114 and $117.75.
The price range on the GDRs was $11.5 to $12.5, the sources said.

The issue is lead managed by Merrill Lynch International, with a selling syndicate formed by ING Barings, Robert Fleming and Co., Paribas Capital Markets and UBS Ltd. Roadshows will take place in the United States, Europe and elsewhere, a source said.
